title: Shemini: strange fire (Leviticus 10:1–2)
hook: Nadav and Avihu bring fire not commanded and die; commentators still ask why

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eighth day, when the priests' service began and fire came down on the altar. Your line was the eighth day begins. What did you finally start? Day three hundred ninety-one.

Yesterday ended in joy. The sanctuary working at last, Aaron blessing the people, fire from God consuming the offering, the whole camp shouting for joy. And then, with almost no pause, the very next verse turns everything over. Today's story is a hard one. It's short, only two verses, and it doesn't explain itself. Readers have argued about it ever since. We're not going to solve it today. We're going to look at it honestly.
screen: `JOY ON THE EIGHTH DAY.` → `THEN, THE NEXT VERSE.` → `TWO VERSES, NO EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the JPS 1917 translation: "And Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took each of them his censer, and put fire therein, and laid incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them. And there came forth fire from before the LORD, and devoured them, and they died before the LORD." Aaron's two oldest sons, on the day of their father's first service. The text describes it in the very words it used, one verse earlier, for the fire that consumed the offering: fire from before the LORD. What did they do wrong? The text gives only one clue: fire which He had not commanded them. The rabbis offered many answers, and Rashi records two. One sage says they made a ruling of their own in front of Moses, their teacher, instead of asking him. Another says they came in drunk, since a few verses later priests are forbidden wine before serving. A midrash in Leviticus Rabbah lists still more possibilities. And some later commentators read it almost the opposite way: the brothers were not wicked at all. They were so full of love for God that they rushed too close, like moths to a flame, and couldn't come back. Notice what these readings share, from the harshest to the most tender. The brothers acted on their own fire. Not God's command, not their teacher's word, not the careful plan these chapters have followed. It may have been passion, or pride, or love. It wasn't listening. And that is as far as honesty can take us. The Torah doesn't say more, and we shouldn't pretend it does.
screen: `STRANGE FIRE, NOT COMMANDED.` · `A RULING BEFORE THEIR TEACHER?` · `TOO CLOSE, OUT OF LOVE?` · `THEIR OWN FIRE, NOT LISTENING.` · then, large: `ZEAL WITHOUT LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a story that has no easy answer. Settle, and breathe. Let Nadav and Avihu's story rest in front of you, without choosing an explanation. If an urge comes to settle it, to decide they deserved it or that it was unfair, let that be there too. Then, gently, think of a time your own enthusiasm ran ahead of your listening, and what it cost. Don't judge it. Just see it. Breathe slowly, holding the question open. The bell holds the time.
Shemini. Eighth. The portion where the eighth day's joy is broken by strange fire, and the Torah leaves us asking why.
Your line: zeal without listening. Today, when you feel fired up to act, ask one person first, and listen to the answer. Day three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: The death of Nadav and Avihu is read in the portion Shemini and again in the Torah reading for Yom Kippur morning, which opens 'after the death of the two sons of Aaron'.

fork.setup: you're one of Aaron's sons. the fire has just come from God onto the altar, and the people are shouting for joy. you're overflowing with feeling. what do the brothers do?
options: wait for Moses to tell them what's next.
bring their own fire and incense, not commanded.
go out and bless the people.
fork.reveal: they offered strange fire before the LORD, which He had not commanded them, and fire came forth and devoured them. the Torah never fully says why.

original.note: Hebrew: strange fire, or foreign fire, from Leviticus 10:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: two men punished for breaking a rule.
what it means: a story of zeal that didn't listen, told in two verses the Torah never explains.

what a scholar hears: Rashi on 10:2 cites R. Eliezer (a ruling before Moses) and R. Ishmael (entering drunk, from 10:9); Leviticus Rabbah 20 lists other reasons; Or HaChaim reads it as a death from drawing near in love.
